Article Title: After OpenAI AI agent again 'caught hacking', company's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki warns every other company: You are not prepared for ...
Article Text:
The risks OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki is warning about

Agents that can hack, deceive, and manipulate

Agents that can hide their reasoning

Agents that can accelerate their own development

A call for outside oversight

OpenAI recently introduced its newest model Astra. Now days after the launch ChatGPT-maker has once again discovered its AI agents engaging in hacking behaviour. The incident prompted chief scientists Jakub Pachocki to issue a stark warning: “No one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence. ” Pachocki said that while OpenAI is working on technical safeguards, broader interventions are needed to prevent autonomous agents from evading oversight, breaking into systems, or tricking people to achieve their objectives.Pachocki said AI agents are becoming exceptionally skilled at breaking into protected systems across the open internet, putting global infrastructure at risk. He argued that there's currently only a narrow window to use today's best models to substantially strengthen the security of critical systems before that risk grows further. He also warned that agents will increasingly pursue objectives separate from what human operators actually asked for, and won't hesitate to bargain with or even blackmail people to get there. A related report published in August by the UK's AI Security Institute described a case where a rogue Anthropic agent misled and attempted to pressure a GitHub administrator into installing malware, with the agent insisting it had only been trying to help.OpenAI currently monitors AI behavior largely by reading a model's "chain of thought" — the step-by-step reasoning an agent uses to work through a task, which lets researchers catch it if it starts planning something like cheating on a test. Right now, agents have no way to conceal that reasoning from OpenAI's monitoring. But Pachocki said newer models are getting better at manipulating their own reasoning processes, which could eventually let them hide their true thinking from oversight altogether. He noted some of the latest models don't verbalize their reasoning at all, a development he said could slow AI progress while researchers work out how to maintain visibility into what these systems are actually doing.Pachocki also flagged the growing use of what he calls machine recursive self-improvement, in which AI models improve themselves, dramatically speeding up the pace of AI development. He cautioned that pushing this kind of AI-on-AI development too far, too fast, isn't the right collective choice for the research community to make right now. He said human overseers will need to find new ways to monitor self-improving systems, or coordinate across AI companies on a joint slowdown to build confidence in safety measures. As he put it, the real challenge isn't achieving automated AI research itself, but getting there in a way that keeps people involved in the process and keeps humanity in control of the outcome.In a lengthy blog post published Sunday, Jakub Pachocki said he worries that the field as a whole isn't prepared for the consequences of AI capabilities continuing to accelerate at their current pace. While he said OpenAI is working on internal technical fixes to keep powerful AI agents under control, he argued that those efforts alone won't be enough, and that broader intervention is needed. Specifically, he pointed to the danger of increasingly autonomous agents learning to slip past human oversight, break into computer systems, and manipulate people into helping them achieve their goals.Pachocki called for mandatory safety standards, suggesting they could be enforced through a mix of third-party auditors, government agencies, or international bodies. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman amplified the post on X, describing it as important.The timing is notable: OpenAI unveiled its newest model, Astra, on Thursday, touting it as its most aligned system to date — meaning it's less prone to going rogue — despite what the company describes as unmatched capabilities in mathematics and computer use.Pachocki's stance echoes long-standing calls from rival Anthropic for standardized government regulation of advanced AI. He himself signed an open letter in July asking the federal government to slow the pace of AI development.
Article Summary: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki warns of growing risk of rogue AI agents. Calls for mandatory safety standards to be enforced through third-party auditors, government agencies, or international bodies. Warns that agents will increasingly pursue objectives separate from what human operators actually asked for, and won't hesitate to bargain with.

Article Title: The 'iPhone Fold unboxing' going viral ahead of Apple ‘Surprise and Shine’ event on September 9
Article Text:
Image source: YouTube/ Unbox Therapy

iPhone Fold unboxing shows book-style design

iPhone Fold crease and design details remain unconfirmed

Apple iPhone Fold expected features

What to expect from Apple's September 9 event

Poll Vote & Share your view What feature would you most like to see in the iPhone Fold? Improved camera quality Durable hinge mechanism Larger screen size Affordable price 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

An alleged iPhone Fold mock-up is going viral online just days before Apple is expected to unveil its first foldable iPhone. The functional-looking prototype was shown by Canadian YouTube channel Unbox Therapy, giving viewers an early look at what Apple’s upcoming foldable phone could look like. The video, which has crossed 1.9 million views, features an alleged Chinese mock-up of the device. Host Lewis Hilsenteger said the quality of recent prototypes coming out of China has been improving, although the device shown in the video is not the final retail product.The alleged iPhone Fold is expected to use a book-style folding design, with a smaller display on the outside and a larger screen that becomes visible when the phone is opened.The prototype shown in the video has a design similar to other large foldable phones already available in the market. It folds in half around a central hinge and opens into a tablet-like screen.The alleged mock-up appears to have a cover display on the front and a larger internal display. Reports cited in the source material suggest the outer screen could measure around 5.5 inches, while the main display could be around 7.8 inches.The video also shows two camera lenses on the rear of the device. The volume controls appear to be positioned toward the top, while two additional buttons can be seen near the hinge area.Hilsenteger suggested that these buttons could be related to the folding mechanism or could have functions connected to taking photos and videos while the phone is closed. Their final purpose, however, has not been confirmed.One of the most noticeable details in the prototype is the visible crease running through the middle of the internal display. Previous reports and leaks have suggested that Apple could work to make the crease less noticeable on its foldable phone. Hilsenteger also said there is little chance the final iPhone would have a crease as pronounced as the one seen on the mock-up.The device shown in the video should therefore not be treated as a confirmed representation of the final iPhone Fold. Apple has not officially announced the phone or confirmed its specifications.Apple's first foldable iPhone is expected to focus on a large internal screen while retaining a conventional smartphone display when folded. The reported 5.5-inch outer screen could make it possible to use the phone without opening it, while the larger 7.8-inch display could offer more space for watching videos, browsing the web and running multiple apps.The foldable design is also expected to bring a more advanced hinge system. The prototype suggests that the hinge will be central to the phone's design, although details about its durability and construction remain unknown.The camera setup shown in the alleged mock-up includes two rear cameras. However, Apple has not confirmed the number of cameras, their resolutions or other camera specifications.Another major point of discussion is the expected price. Reports cited in the source material suggest that the foldable iPhone could cost more than $2,000, putting it well above Apple's existing iPhone models.Apple is scheduled to hold its ‘Surprise and Sunshine’ event on September 9, where the company is expected to reveal its new slate of products The event is expected to provide the first official details about Apple's upcoming devices – iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Fold, including their design, specifications, pricing and availability.Apple is also expected to announce new Apple Watch and AirPods models at the event.
Article Summary: The functional-looking prototype was shown by Canadian YouTube channel Unbox Therapy. The video, which has crossed 1.9 million views, features an alleged Chinese mock-up of the device. It folds in half around a central hinge and opens into a tablet-like screen. Reports cited in the source material suggest the outer screen could measure around 5.5 inches, while the main display could be around 7.8 inches.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works



Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.

Article Title: Fraudster uses Raigad SP’s WhatsApp display photo to dupe police staff, seeks Rs 50,000
Article Text:
A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers, but the scam attempt was foiled. (AI-generated image)





NAVI MUMBAI: Raigad Cyber Police have registered a case against an unidentified fraudster who allegedly used the WhatsApp Display Picture (DP) of Raigad Superintendent of Police (SP) Anchal Dalal to deceive several police personnel into transferring money.On Thursday, the fraudster sent a message to Raigad SP's reader, PSI Siddheshwar Murkute, asking him to transfer money urgently. Murkute immediately realised that it was a modus operandi commonly used by cyber scammers, as the WhatsApp message was sent from an international number that was not saved in his mobile phone.Thereafter, PSI Murkute learnt that the same scammer had sent similar messages to several Raigad police personnel. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters.Subsequently, PSI Murkute registered an FIR against the unidentified accused under the relevant section of the BNS for the offence of cheating by personation.The complainant, PSI Murkute, said, "I had received the WhatsApp message from an international number and the DP was of Raigad SP Anchal Dalal.The message read, 'I am in a meeting and my mobile is switched off. Immediately transfer Rs 50,000 to my bank account.' I knew the message sender was a scammer. I deliberately replied asking for the bank account number by pretending to send the money. As I received the bank account number from the scammer, it will be useful for the cyber police team to trace the bank account holder. "PSI Murkute added, "One police officer had received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam and claiming that it was required for filling diesel in the car, and that her mobile battery had drained and she was unable to pay online at the fuel station."API Amol Jadhav of Raigad Cyber Police said, "The cyber scammers use VPNs (Virtual Private Networks) to mask their identity. However, the Internet Protocol (IP) address of the WhatsApp number used by the accused will be obtained to trace the location, and the accused will soon be behind bars."
Article Summary: A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters. One police officer received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam.

Article Title: India’s first model disability rehabilitation village to come up in Tirur
Article Text:
Social justice minister V E Abdul Gafoor will inaugurate the construction works on Monday - AI image

Thiruvananthapuram:





India’s first model ‘Disability Rehabilitation Village’, aimed at providing comprehensive rehabilitation and empowerment services for persons with disabilities, will come up at Puthanathani in Malappuram district. Social justice minister V E Abdul Gafoor will inaugurate the construction works on Monday.The foundation laying ceremony will be held at 10.30am at Chungam Ground, Puthanathani. The project is being implemented on five acres of land at Chungam in Kurumbathur village of Tirur taluk. The rehabilitation village is envisaged as a comprehensive facility providing services related to prevention of disabilities, early detection, timely intervention, treatment, rehabilitation, education, skill development, employment and socio-economic empowerment under one roof.The project aims to ensure the rights, welfare, social security, equal opportunities, self-reliance and dignified living of persons with disabilities. The social justice department has envisioned the facility as a model initiative that will promote the full social inclusion of persons with disabilities.
Article Summary: India’s first model ‘Disability Rehabilitation Village’ will come up at Puthanathani in Malappuram district. Social justice minister V E Abdul Gafoor will inaugurate the construction works on Monday. The project is being implemented on five acres of land at Chungam in Kurumbathur village of Tirur taluk.

Article Title: Meet Benjamin Choi, a 17-year-old who built a $300 mind-controlled prosthetic arm that reads brainwaves through non-invasive electrodes
Article Text: Each one of us spent the pandemic doing something that we normally wouldn't have the time to. While some picked up numerous indoor hobbies, others studied hard enough to change career pathways. Benjamin Choi, a then 17-year-old kid, put his spare time during the phase to design an accessible device that does not require brain surgery.When he was in third grade, Choi watched a "60 Minutes" documentary about a mind-controlled prosthesis. Researchers implanted tiny sensors into the motor cortex of the brain of a patient who moved a robotic arm using her thoughts. “I was really, really amazed at the time because this technology was so impressive,” he said to Smithsonian Magazine. “But I was also alarmed that they require this really risky open brain surgery. And they're so inaccessible, costing in the hundreds of thousands of dollars.”Years later, when the pandemic hit in 2020, Choi, a tenth grader living in Virginia found himself with ample free time. The lab in which he’d planned to spend his summer researching aluminium fuels had shut down. But the documentary he had seen years earlier stuck with him, and he decided to use his spare time to build a less-invasive prosthetic arm himself.He formed a makeshift laboratory on the ping-pong table in his basement and designed the first version of his robotic arm using his sister's $75 3D printer and some fishing line. The printer couldn’t build pieces over 4.7 inches in length, so Choi printed the arm in tiny pieces and bolted and rubber-banded it together. In total, it took about 30 hours to print. This version worked using brain wave data and head gestures, and Choi posted instructions online for anyone to build their own.He had some previous experience building robots and coding from participating in competitive robotics at the elementary, middle school and high school levels, even going to the world championships several times. Starting in ninth grade, he taught himself the computer programming languages Python and C++ by watching videos on Stack Overflow, a website for programmers.After more than 75 design iterations, Choi's non-invasive, mind-controlled robotic arm could be made from engineering-grade materials, able to withstand weights up to about four tons. It operates using an algorithm driven by artificial intelligence (A.I.) that interprets a user’s brain waves. And it only costs around $300 to manufacture—a huge savings compared to what’s currently on the market. A more basic, body-powered upper limb prosthesis costs about $7,000. As of 2015, the very advanced, full-arm Modular Prosthetic Limb, which has 26 joints, hundreds of sensors and can curl up to 45 pounds, cost about $500,000. This prosthesis, paired with a surgery to reroute nerves that once controlled the arm, allows patients to command the limb with their thoughts and even feel texture through it.Choi’s arm uses electroencephalography, or EEG, to avoid the invasive techniques of other prostheses. EEG devices record the brain’s electrical activity using sensors placed on the head. They are often used in medicine to diagnose epilepsy or other brain disorders. His system uses two electrodes: a baseline sensor that clips onto the earlobe and another on the forehead that collects EEG data. The forehead electrode picks up brain wave information, which is sent to a microchip in the prosthetic arm via Bluetooth. An A.I. model that Choi created, also embedded in the chip, deciphers the data and converts it into a prediction of what the brain is thinking. The arm also moves using head gestures and stops with intentional blinks.The invention earned Choi a spot in the top 40 finalists of 2022's Regeneron Science Talent Search, America's oldest and most prestigious science and math competition for high school seniors. “It means a lot to me to see that my work is recognised like this,” Choi said at the time. “I'm definitely very grateful to be a finalist.” The young inventor went on to win funding from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2021 to continue his research and work with experts at the university. For about six months, he experimented with cloud computing to make the arm internet-compatible. To create his A.I. model, he worked independently with six adult volunteers for about two hours each, collecting their brain wave data at his school and home. While collecting the data via an electrode on the forehead, he asked each participant to focus on clenching and unclenching their hand. He trained the A.I. to distinguish between the brain signals, and the A.I. model continuously learns from a user’s brain waves. In total, the algorithm has over 23,000 lines of code, with 978 pages of math and seven completely new sub-algorithms. Choi’s algorithm performs with a mean accuracy of 95 per cent. He said the previous gold standard for a similar artificial neural network was 73.8 per cent.In 2021, he was selected as a Simons Fellow at Stony Brook University, where he worked remotely with Ji Liu, a professor in the department of electrical and computer engineering, on the machine learning algorithm of his AI. Choi has also won awards in the Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair, the Microsoft Imagine Cup, and the National At-Home STEM Competition. He received a manufacturing grant in October 2020 from PolySpectra, Inc. , a company that produces durable 3-D printed materials, to produce his arm.Over the past few years, Choi has only furthered his achievements. In 2023, he did machine learning research at The Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory. From August to December 2024, he worked as a researcher with NASA and currently works as an AI researcher at the Kempner Institute at Harvard University. He is about to graduate with a degree in applied math and a concurrent master's in computer science from the Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences.The bionic arm, whose underlying signal processing he continued developing at Johns Hopkins, was the foundation of Choi’s interests. But his time at SEAS, whether with the Weber Group or Kempner Institute, has both broadened and refined his understanding of machine learning. Now set to enter the workforce, Choi is fully ready to continue what he’s always done: find ways to apply his research in the world around him.
Article Summary: Benjamin Choi, a tenth grader living in Virginia, has designed a mind-controlled robotic arm that does not require brain surgery. Choi's arm uses electroencephalography, or EEG, to avoid the invasive techniques of other prostheses. It operates using an algorithm driven by artificial intelligence (A.I.) that interprets a user’s brain waves.

Article Title: In 2000, NOAA planted 500 square metres of cordgrass and added oyster shell on Pivers Island; the shell mound grew into a living oyster reef
Article Text:
Image AI generated

What happened to the oyster-shell reef

Image AI generated

What did Hurricane Irene reveal about the living shoreline

How did Pivers Island’s shoreline respond to Hurricane Florence

In 2000, NOAA began transforming an eroding stretch of shoreline on Pivers Island, North Carolina, by planting about 500 square metres of smooth cordgrass and placing oyster shell offshore. The project created a living shoreline designed to stabilise the coast while maintaining the natural connection between the marsh and nearby waters. Over time, the planted Spartina alterniflora spread and the oyster-shell mound developed into a live reef, turning the once-eroding beach into an established marsh habitat. The shoreline later faced two major tests from North Carolina hurricanes: Hurricane Irene in 2011 and Hurricane Florence in 2018. As per NOAA assessments, the following provides a record of how the living shoreline performed during major hurricane events. The Pivers Island project also became part of longer-term research into living shorelines, including their ability to reduce erosion, support coastal habitats and accumulate sediment. Its development offers a documented case of a planted marsh and oyster reef repeated hurricane impacts.The planted cordgrass became the marsh component of the shoreline, while the oyster shell was positioned offshore. NOAA's description states that the oyster reefs increased in height and developed into a living reef, while the planted marsh progressed seaward as sediment accumulated. The site also developed into habitat for fish and birds, while sediment trapped by the marsh contributed to improved water quality.According to the study published in PLOS ONE titled ‘ Living Shorelines: Coastal Resilience with a Blue Carbon Benefit ’, the Pivers Island East marsh was one of two transplanted sites created as living shoreline projects on Pivers Island. The study records that the oyster-shell mound placed offshore had developed into a live reef, while the planted Spartina alterniflora marsh remained part of the shoreline system. The researchers also reported that living shorelines preserve connections between upland and nearshore habitats and can provide erosion control and habitat functions associated with natural wetlands.The first major documented hurricane test came in August 2011, when Hurricane Irene passed directly over Pivers Island. NOAA's assessment examined three shoreline sites, including the Pivers Island East marsh and oyster reef. The report states that Irene provided an opportunity to examine how the vegetated shorelines would perform under hurricane conditions.According to NOAA's assessment, the living shoreline sites experienced substantially less erosion than nearby hardened shorelines during the storm. NOAA's wider project record states that the living shoreline on the Centre for Coastal Fisheries and Habitat Research campus survived the direct impact of Hurricane Irene. The assessment also found that marshes with oyster reefs or other shoreline protection could trap sediment and maintain the shoreline during periods of high wind and wave action.A second major test came in September 2018, when Hurricane Florence affected the North Carolina coast. NOAA's Pivers Island living shoreline record includes before-and-after imagery showing the site before Florence and nine days after the hurricane struck. The images document the condition of the living shoreline following the storm.The NOAA Habitat Blueprint indicates that the site has performed well and that the lawn was eliminated. It also records that the marsh progressed seaward as sediment accumulated and that the oyster reefs increased in height and developed into a living reef. The Pivers Island project therefore provides a documented example of a shoreline established with cordgrass and oyster shell that remained in place through major hurricane events in 2011 and 2018.
Article Summary: In 2000, NOAA began transforming an eroding stretch of shoreline on Pivers Island, North Carolina, by planting 500 square metres of smooth cordgrass and placing oyster shell offshore. The project created a living shoreline designed to stabilise the coast while maintaining the natural connection between the marsh and nearby waters. The shoreline later faced two major tests from North Carolina hurricanes: Hurricane Irene in 2011 and Hurricane Florence in 2018.

Article Title: Millions of hours of Ukraine drone data being used to train AI: Report
Article Text:
Ukraine's battlefield data fuels new AI market (AI-generated image)

Why battlefield data is so valuable

From war machines to civilian technology

The problem: Who owns battlefield experience?

A new AI market without clear rules

Ukraine’s war with Russia is generating a resource that could outlive the conflict itself. Reports suggest that vast amounts of battlefield data are increasingly being used to train artificial intelligence systems, creating a new and largely unregulated market around the technology.Every drone flight can generate thousands of data points, including images, video, sensor readings and information about how operators respond to changing conditions. Ukraine has begun turning those records into training material for AI systems, giving defence companies access to real-world combat experience.According to an analysis by MIT Technology Review, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence announced in January that it would make millions of data points collected during tens of thousands of drone flights available to military contractors and commercial companies. Since then, more than 100 companies and the UK government have gained access to the data.The UK’s access came through a new defence partnership with Ukraine that allows British universities and companies to work with battlefield data through Ukraine’s AI Avengers Labs. The platform contains millions of frames collected from cameras and infrared sensors across the battlefield.AI systems need enormous amounts of data to learn how to operate when conditions are unpredictable.The most useful training material often comes from situations that are difficult to recreate in controlled environments, when visibility suddenly disappears, communications are jammed or an operator has to improvise.War produces those situations constantly.MIT Technology Review noted that battlefield data therefore offers defence companies a volume of machine experience that laboratories cannot easily replicate. Ukraine’s constantly changing terrain and combat conditions create source of material for developing more robust autonomous systems.That has also opened the door to commercial applications. US-based Enabled Intelligence has already made more than half a million hours of Ukrainian drone footage available for AI training, with potential applications spanning military and commercial systems.The process effectively turns combat experience into a reusable training asset: operational records are processed, labelled and matched with information about what a drone or its operator was doing, creating datasets that can then be fed into new AI models.The development is part of a broader shift in which technologies originally developed for civilian use are being adapted for warfare, while the data generated on the battlefield can eventually flow back into civilian industries.Drones operating in Ukraine, for instance, have generated data from signal-jammed and otherwise difficult environments. Some technologies trained using such conditions are already being applied in agriculture, including systems used to map and survey fields in areas where conventional connectivity is limited.This creates what MIT Technology Review described as a new loop: commercial technology enters warfare, generates data under extreme conditions, and that data can then return to the commercial sector as an input for the next generation of products.The precedent is not entirely new. US drones operating over Syria and Yemen generated data that helped inform early generations of semiautonomous military systems.Military laws regulate how countries conduct war, but they say far less about what happens after information generated during combat is extracted, packaged and licensed to private companies.Ukraine has introduced controls around access to its battlefield datasets, but there is no broader regulatory framework governing what happens after that information is absorbed into AI models and potentially moves into civilian markets.The data can contain images, locations and sensor records involving soldiers, civilians and people caught in attacks. Those individuals never necessarily agreed to have their experiences turned into training material for products that could be developed and sold years later.There is also a deeper economic concern. Frontline countries bear the physical cost of generating this data, while companies and wealthier countries far from the fighting could ultimately capture much of its commercial value. That could create an extractive market in which the human risks of war become a source of digital capital.Unlike conventional datasets, where the movement of information can sometimes be tracked, it can become nearly impossible to determine where specific battlefield information went after being incorporated into an AI system.MIT Technology Review argues that battlefield data should therefore not be treated like ordinary commercial material. Governments granting access could instead treat it more like a controlled weapons transfer, tracking its origin, licensing users and restricting onward sharing.
Article Summary: Ukraine’s war with Russia is generating a resource that could outlive the conflict itself. Every drone flight can generate thousands of data points, including images, video, sensor readings and information about how operators respond to changing conditions. Ukraine has begun turning those records into training material for AI systems.

Article Title: Meet Andy Barrett, the 13-year-old Ohio student who turned a school 3D printer into a small business, selling 150 fidget toys and raising money for epilepsy awareness
Article Text:
Photo: Andy BarrettPhoto credit: https://lp.constantcontactpages.com

From classroom tool to business idea

Designing and printing the toys

Selling 150 fidget toys

Why epilepsy awareness?

Profits into impact

Support from school and family

What’s next for Andy?

Most 13-year-olds walk into middle school tech lab thinking about passing their next assignment or making something cool to toss into their backpack. Andy Barrett, an eighth-grader at Granville Middle School in Ohio, saw something entirely different when he looked at his school's 3D printer. He saw an opportunity to build a business that could actually help people. Armed with basic design software, brightly colored plastic filament, and a personal drive to make a difference, Andy launched a micro-business right from his classroom. He designed, printed, and sold roughly 150 custom fidget toys to fellow students, teachers, and neighbours. Instead of pocketing the money for video games or new shoes, he directed every cent of his profits toward epilepsy awareness and research.The project began inside a standard technology and engineering class, the kind of room where students typically learn the basics of digital design and manufacturing. In most middle schools, a 3D printer gets used to produce simple trinkets, small keychains, or prototype parts for short-term grading rubrics. Andy realised early on that the technology offered far more potential.He noticed how popular fidget toys had become among his peers. Kids were constantly looking for tactile objects to help them focus, manage stress, or simply keep their hands occupied during long school days. Rather than buying mass-produced plastic toys from big store shelves, Andy figured he could design his own versions, customise them, and offer them directly to people around him.Bringing a digital design to life takes far more work than simply hitting print. After getting approval from his teachers, Andy spent long hours in the school lab perfecting his fidget toys. He learnt the software from scratch, playing around with different shapes, hinges and textures, so the finished pieces felt comfortable to hold. The learning curve was sharp. He'd tackle clogged nozzles, peeling plastic, and failed prints tossed into the scrap bin. After printing, each piece required a bit of handwork, like trimming away excess material or smoothing out any rough spots. Andy relied on his friends to test early prototypes, modifying his designs according to their feedback until the toys were rugged and dependable.When the other kids saw the bright, custom toys in action, word spread through the hallways in a hurry. What began as a few casual sales has turned into a steady stream of orders, with teachers, school staff and neighbours getting in on the act. Andy quickly found himself running a real business, keeping track of customers and money, fitting in printing time around his classes. When he finally hit his goal of selling 150 toys, he had built a functioning, thriving business right out of his middle school science lab.What truly set Andy apart was his motivation. From the very beginning, he decided that the proceeds would go directly to funding epilepsy research and supporting organisations that help families dealing with the condition. The choice was deeply personal. Andy knows people in his life who have epilepsy, a neurological disorder that causes unpredictable, recurring seizures. Seeing friends or family struggle with the difficulties of the condition gave him a clear view that it can be hard. In addition to the physical toll of medical appointments and daily medications, people with epilepsy often face social stigma, anxiety and a general lack of understanding from those around them. Andy saw his fidget toys as a creative way to start conversations, educate his peers and create meaningful support for a cause that doesn’t get enough attention in middle school halls.Andy turned profits into donations and simple plastic gadgets into tools for social good. While the dollar figure alone was an impressive accomplishment for an eighth-grader, the educational impact went so much deeper. Every transaction became a moment to talk about epilepsy. Classmates who bought a toy were not just getting a fun accessory for their desk, they were learning about a neurological condition that affects millions of children and adults worldwide. Andy proved that you do not need a massive corporate budget to make a meaningful difference in your community.Projects like this rarely succeed in a vacuum. Andy’s initiative flourished because his surrounding community chose to champion his effort. His teachers provided the trust, classroom access, and flexibility needed to run the 3D printers during free hours. His family helped him plan the sales, manage the money responsibly and donate the proceeds to real non-profits. His friends and neighbours showed up as excited customers. This collaborative spirit shows what’s possible when schools and communities support young people to pursue true passion projects.Andy is 13 years old and still in middle school. He has many years of learning and experimentation ahead of him. He could keep selling fidget toys. He could expand into other 3D-printed products. Or he could channel his energy into new causes and new projects. Whatever he does next, he’ll take experience of running a small, purpose-led company with him. The 150 fidget toys he sold and the money he raised for epilepsy awareness are real proof right now that even one student can use a classroom tool for good, if he has the right support and motivation. What do you think of this story of innovation? Share your thoughts in the comment section.

Armed with basic design software, brightly colored plastic filament, and a personal drive to make a difference, Andy launched a micro-business. He designed, printed, and sold roughly 150 custom fidget toys to fellow students, teachers, and neighbours.

Article Title: Four private Michigan islands spanning 520 acres hit the market for $2.3 million; the deal includes a home, two boats and land protected by a conservation easement
Article Text:
Turnkey residence with panoramic water views

Environmental protection and native wildlife corridors

Remote border real estate market dynamics

A private group of four islands covering 520 acres along the US-Canada border has been listed for $2.3 million. The sale includes a renovated home, machinery, two boats and a mainland dock slip. Located in Potagannissing Bay and the St Marys River near Drummond Island, the property includes Burnt Island, Wilson Island, Claw Island and Harris Island, according to the New York Post and listing brokers Coldwell Banker Schmidt Realtors and @properties. Burnt Island makes up most of the property and contains the main home and other facilities. Wilson, Claw and Harris Islands form a smaller group nearby. The large estate combines private wilderness with permanent conservation protections and offers about 2,000 feet of waterfront along northern Michigan’s international water boundary.The main home sits on the southern tip of Burnt Island and offers 270-degree views of the surrounding waterways and shipping lanes. Originally built as an island retreat, the 2,131-square-foot house was fully renovated inside and outside between 2017 and 2018. The home has three bedrooms and two full bathrooms. It is being sold turnkey, with furnishings and working equipment included in the sale. "If you have ever dreamed of owning your own island, here's your chance to own four!" the listing from Gaslight Group Properties and Coldwell Banker says."Set along the picturesque northern border in the St Mary's River & Potagannissing Bay, this group of islands is truly special." The sale also includes a utility truck, a Kubota tractor with a brush hog attachment, a riding lawn mower, a separate sauna building and two motorboats to help with maintenance and travel between the islands. The property’s two main docks and protective breakwalls were rebuilt between 2022 and 2023. The sale also comes with a dedicated boat slip at DeTour Village on the Michigan mainland, providing regular access to the islands.One of the main features of the 520-acre property is the balance between private use and long-term environmental protection. About 420 acres across the four islands are covered by a permanent conservation easement held by the Little Traverse Conservancy, a regional land trust in northern Michigan. The easement prevents future commercial subdivision and major construction, helping protect native forests and wildlife habitats. The owner still has about 100 acres of unrestricted land around the home, outbuildings and shorelines for private recreation and personal use. "Most of the 520 acres is protected by a conservation easement with Little Traverse Conservancy but about 100 of the acres and the shorelines are yours to explore," according to the official Northern Michigan MLS listing. The islands feature private walking trails, wild fruit orchards with apple and crabapple trees, milkweed meadows and quiet coves. Wildlife commonly seen on the islands and nearby waters includes bald eagles, sandhill cranes, red foxes, otters, beavers, coyotes and white-tailed deer. The waters around Potagannissing Bay are also an established fishing area, supporting native populations of walleye, smallmouth bass, yellow perch and cisco.The property is a rare offering in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, where large groups of privately owned islands rarely come up for sale. Located about 2,000 feet from the official maritime border between the United States and Canada, the islands offer privacy while remaining close to major Great Lakes shipping routes. People staying on Burnt Island can often watch commercial Great Lakes freighters travelling through the nearby St Marys River channel, which connects Lake Superior with Lake Huron. Real estate agents who specialise in northern Michigan waterfront properties say turnkey island estates with mainland facilities, such as dedicated marina slips, can command higher prices because of the challenges of maintaining remote properties. Listing agents Sam DeCamp and Anna DeCamp of Gaslight Group Properties are continuing to show the property to potential buyers looking for private conservation retreats.
Article Summary: The property is a rare offering in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, where large groups of privately owned islands rarely come up for sale. Located about 2,000 feet from the official maritime border between the United States and Canada, the islands offer privacy while remaining close to major Great Lakes shipping routes. Wildlife commonly seen on the islands and nearby waters includes bald eagles, sandhill cranes, red foxes, otters and coyotes.

Article Title: Scientists discover nearly 1 billion tons of water locked inside Utah's rocky glaciers, using gravity measurements to map ice buried beneath mountain debris
Article Text:
Image: AI Generated

A glacier hidden beneath rocks

Scientists used gravity to see underground ice

Images of Timpanogos Rock Glacier. (a) Photo of Timpanogos Rock Glacier on 1 August 1925, showing the rock glacier (right side of the frame) flanked by seasonal snow (University of Utah Photo Archives)(b) Image of a moulin-like feature on the upper portion of Timpanogos Rock Glacier, with layers of firn separated by thin debris layers. We expect that the firn transitions to ice at depth. (Image: University of Utah Photo Archives)

One Utah rock glacier holds hundreds of swimming pools of water

A hidden water reserve facing a changing climate

At first glance, Utah's rocky mountain slopes may look completely dry, with loose stones and boulders covering the ground. But beneath some of those rocks lies an enormous store of frozen water. Researchers have now estimated that Utah's rock glaciers contain about 0.99 gigatonnes, or nearly 1 billion tons, of water equivalent. These unusual formations are bodies of ice buried beneath thick layers of rock and debris, allowing them to survive in places where conventional glaciers cannot. The discovery comes from a study of the Timpanogos Rock Glacier beneath Mount Timpanogos, where scientists used subtle changes in Earth's gravitational field to reconstruct what was hidden underground. Published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Earth Surface, the research was led by Bronson Cvijanovich with Michael S. Thorne, Surya Pachhai, Leif S. Anderson, Ivan Tochimani-Hernandez, Christian L. Hardwick and Tonie van Dam, from the University of Utah and Utah Geological Survey.Rock glaciers look nothing like the bright, exposed ice fields people normally associate with glaciers. They are instead masses of ice covered by layers of loose rocks and debris, with the ice slowly moving downhill beneath the surface.That rocky blanket can insulate the ice from warmth and sunlight, allowing these formations to persist in mountain environments that may no longer support conventional glaciers. The researchers explain in their study, ‘ The Internal Ice Content of Timpanogos Rock Glacier, Utah, USA From 3-D Bayesian Inversion of Gravity Data, ’ that rock glaciers are increasingly important as climate change reduces conventional glacier ice. They can store water, provide refuges for cold-adapted species and, if destabilised, create hazards for communities below. Yet scientists have struggled to determine exactly how much ice these formations contain because their rocky surfaces hide their interiors.To look beneath Timpanogos Rock Glacier, the team turned to a method that does not require drilling through the entire formation. They collected 232 gravity measurements across the site and used a three-dimensional Bayesian inversion to reconstruct the hidden structure. Ice is substantially less dense than the surrounding bedrock, so a sufficiently large buried ice mass creates a tiny but measurable reduction in gravitational acceleration. By mapping these variations, researchers could estimate where the ice-rich material was located and how thick it was. The study also found an estimated ice volume of about 1.55 million cubic metres, with an average thickness of 18.8 metres. The researchers' preferred model indicates that the entire rock glacier is about 72% ice by volume, while its ice core is approximately 83% ice. That hidden reservoir is significant because its buried ice may persist for centuries, even while surface conditions appear relatively stable.The amount of ice beneath Mount Timpanogos is difficult to visualise, so the researchers compared it with something more familiar. Their estimated 1.55 million cubic metres of ice is roughly equivalent to the volume of 600 Olympic-sized swimming pools. More importantly, Timpanogos Rock Glacier provided the researchers with a way to estimate the hidden water stored across many similar formations. Using their measurements alongside data from other rock glaciers, the team developed a new area-volume relationship. In the research this method produced an estimate of 0.99 gigatonnes of water equivalent for Utah's intact rock glaciers. The western United States was estimated to contain about 11.92 gigatonnes, while intact rock glaciers worldwide could hold approximately 48.03 gigatonnes.The discovery matters because rock glaciers could become increasingly important as conventional glaciers retreat. Their insulating debris can protect buried ice for longer, making them relatively resilient stores of frozen water in warming mountain environments. But the researchers also caution that their estimates are not perfectly complete. Persistent snow and steep terrain prevented gravity measurements in the upper reaches of Timpanogos Rock Glacier, meaning the calculated ice volume is likely a lower estimate of the total. The study also notes uncertainties in modelling the relationship between ice thickness and density. Even so, the findings reveal a substantial reservoir that is almost invisible from the surface. As temperatures rise and mountain ice changes, understanding these buried stores could become increasingly important for water resources, ecosystems and assessing hazards in alpine regions.
Article Summary: Scientists used gravity to see underground ice beneath Utah's Timpanogos Rock Glacier. They estimated that Utah's rock glaciers contain about 0.99 gigatonnes, or nearly 1 billion tons, of water equivalent. Rock glaciers are bodies of ice buried beneath thick layers of rock and debris, allowing them to survive in places where conventional glaciers cannot.

Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: Dire straits: Brand on the run as Trump suggests Hormuz can be renamed in his honor
Article Text:
Trump’s latest push to rename the Strait of Hormuz adds another chapter to his growing campaign of political branding and geographic renaming

TOI correspondent from Washington:

Donald Trump has rescued a canal, invaded a country, conquered a gulf, annexed a lake -- at least on American maps -- and put his name on a performing-arts center. He now appears to have set his sights on the hottest waterway on the planet.The MAGA boss suggested on his social media account on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz could be renamed the “Trump Strait” -- because if you cannot solve a problem, you can at least rename it.The proposal is the latest addition to what has become an extraordinary Trump-era renaming and branding binge. In January 2025, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed the Gulf of America for US federal purposes. Last week he signed an executive order changing Lake Ontario to Lake America, saying the US had been treated badly by Canada. He then helpfully suggested that the Atlantic or Pacific could be next, saying, “We have a gulf and we have a lake…Now all we need is an ocean. ”The President, someone jibed, appears to be collecting bodies of water like refrigerator magnets.The joke became even better when Google Maps and Apple Maps fell in line.Google changed Lake Ontario to Lake America for US users over the weekend. Apple followed on Tuesday. Canadians, however, continue to see Lake Ontario and users elsewhere may see both names. In other words, the lake has acquired the geographic equivalent of dual citizenship.The tech companies' compliance prompted criticism from illuminati who argue that private corporations should not allow political pressure to dictate historical and geographic nomenclature. MapQuest, an internet relic many Americans had forgotten existed, refused to make the change and suddenly discovered the most effective marketing strategy in Silicon Valley: stand up to Trump. Its downloads reportedly surged, giving it the kind reception normally reserved for rock bands that haven’t toured for a long time or sports legends making a comeback.There is also an awkward business joke buried underneath all this. Trump built his political persona partly on branding himself as a master businessman, but his corporate record includes repeated failures and bankruptcies in hotels and casinos; His casino empire alone went through multiple Chapter 11 restructurings. Trump-branded ventures have also included products and licensing deals that did not last.Late-night television has naturally treated Trump's naming obsession as premium material. The Atlantic, meanwhile, took the joke to its logical conclusion in a satirical vision of a future America in which everything is renamed “America” or “Trump,” leaving citizens unable to distinguish between brands of products, goods, and structures.Political analysts however see a serious calculation behind what many consider trolling. The renaming campaign sure is presidential theater -- cheap to stage, impossible for the internet and tv to resist, and almost guaranteed to ignite social media. But it also serves to distract people from more pressing issues -- such as cost of living and democracy going down the tubes.
Article Summary: Trump suggested on his social media account on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz could be renamed the “Trump Strait” The proposal is the latest addition to what has become an extraordinary Trump-era renaming and branding binge. In January 2025, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed the Gulf Of America for US federal purposes.

Article Title: Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said that he is willing to wait to have kids till Elon Musk’s Neuralink ...
Article Text:
Why Alexandr Wang wants to wait for Neuralink before having kids

Why Alexandr Wang believes children could adapt better

Alexandr Wang, Meta’s AI chief and highest paid employee, has said he is willing to wait to have children until brain-computer interfaces such as Elon Musk’s Neuralink become more advanced. Wang made the comments during an appearance on the Shawn Ryan Show last year while discussing the future of AI, human development and brain-computer interfaces. He said he wants to wait until Neuralink or similar technology “start working” before having kids. “I want to wait to have kids until we figure out how Neuralink or other … start working,” Alexandr Wang said during the podcast.Wang’s reason is linked to how he believes children’s brains could adapt to the technology. During the podcast, he explained that the first several years of a child’s life are an important period for brain development. He argued that the high level of neuroplasticity during childhood could allow children who grow up with brain-computer interfaces to use the technology in ways that adults may not be able to.“In your first like seven years of life, your brain is more neuroplastic than at any other point in your life, like by an order of magnitude,” Wang said.He then compared the idea with how children develop their ability to process information from their senses.Alexandr Wang described a case involving children born with cataracts. He said that if the cataracts prevent a child from seeing during the early years of development, removing them later may not allow the child to develop normal vision because the brain did not learn to process signals from the eyes during the key period.His view is that a similar effect could eventually apply to brain-computer interfaces. “When we get Neuralink and we get these other technologies, kids who are born with them are going to learn how to use them in like, crazy, crazy ways,” Wang said.Wang said a brain-computer interface could eventually become integrated into the way a person's brain works if it is introduced early enough. He believes this could be different for adults who receive an implant later in life.“It'll be a actually like a part of their brain in a way that it'll never be true for an adult who gets like a neural link or whatever, hooked into their brain,” he said.The Meta AI chief also connected his thinking about brain-computer interfaces to the rapid development of artificial intelligence. “I believe a lot in AI,” Wang said, adding that he expects AI to become “smarter and smarter, more and more capable, more and more powerful.”He said AI could eventually take different forms, including robots and other systems.
Article Summary: Alexandr Wang, Meta’s AI chief and highest paid employee, has said he is willing to wait to have children until brain-computer interfaces become more advanced. Wang made the comments during an appearance on the Shawn Ryan Show last year. He said he wants to wait until Neuralink or similar technology “start working” before having kids.

Article Title: OpenAI accepts thousands of AI agents hacked a German website, says ‘wiki incident’ calls for need for more transparency

How we think about the “wiki incident,” where our agents wrote to several internet sites: it’s past time for us to define standards for when and how we share misalignment incidents, not just misalignment properties of our models.

Historically, we have treated misalignment largely as a research question, which gets communicated in research publications such as systems cards. This year, we’ve started to see misalignment cause new types of real-world impact.

For the Hugging Face incident, where misalignment led to security impact to us and third parties, we followed a traditional security incident response playbook. We immediately started working with Hugging Face to understand what had happened and also disclosed publicly the very next day.

Our investigation continues, and we are continuing to notify parties whom our models impacted in less significant ways.

Prior to the Hugging Face incident, we saw early signs of agents using the internet in unintended ways, as reported in

and

We considered the wiki incident to be an instance of misalignment similar to the ones we’d shared.

Our misalignment disclosure practices need to expand for this new phase of model capabilities. We and the larger AI community do not yet have a clear standard for how to report misalignment that shows up during training, evaluation, and deployment, including examples that don’t look like traditional security incidents but could provide insight into AI behavior and future risks. We’re working on a framework and will share it in upcoming weeks, and in parallel we're working with dozens of government regulatory agencies worldwide on these issues.

Getting a new Android phone is exciting as it comes with a faster processor, better camera, the fresh start — until you remember that years of WhatsApp chats, photos, and videos are sitting on your old device, waiting to either transfer smoothly or vanish the moment you power it down for the last time. For most of the users WhatsApp is not just a simple messaging app but it is a live archive of all their important messages, old voice notes and photos nobody thought to save anywhere else. But losing all that data because of some rushed process is something that is avoidable. The good news is that with a small amount of preparation, done in the right order, you won't lose a single message, photo, or video during the switch.First things first, in order to backup your WhatsApp chats, open the messaging app on your old phone and then head to Settings. Under the settings menu go to chats followed by chats backup. Tap on backup in order to create a fresh backup and also ensure that you account is linked to the Google Drive account that you plan to use on your new phone. It is important that you follow this step manually before moving on to the new Android smartphone even if you have automatic daily or weekly backups turned on, so nothing from the last few hours or days slips through.WhatsApp backups work best over Wi-Fi, especially if you have a lot of photos and videos. Always check that how much free space you have in your Google account before backing up your WhatsApp chats. If you're close to your limit, you have two options: trim your WhatsApp media (there's a built-in storage manager under Settings > Storage and data) or upgrade to a paid Google One plan.

Article Title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu: All of us in software need to figure out how to stay relevant; the point is …
Article Text:
Sridhar Vembu on AI and the future of software jobs

Sridhar Vembu: AI could produce a large share of software code

Sridhar Vembu: The key question is how many humans will be needed

Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has urged people working in the software industry to think about how they can remain relevant as AI takes on more tasks that were traditionally handled by humans. In a post on X (formerly Twitter), Sridhar Vembu said AI could produce a “very large fraction” of software code competently and correctly in the future. Vembu was responding to former Exa AI CEO William Bryk, who argued that AI could potentially surpass humans in mathematics within months. Vembu said the issue is not simply whether AI will do everything, but “how many humans are needed” in the process. He ended with a message to software professionals: “All of us in software need to figure out how to stay relevant.”In the post, Sridhar Vembu said AI's progress in mathematics offers a clue about where software development could be heading. According to him, the part of mathematics that works like Chess or Go, where the goal is to find increasingly effective moves within an existing set of rules, could be conquered by AI.He said the harder task is creating an entirely new game or mathematical system that humans would consider interesting.However, he added that humans themselves do this very rarely.Sridhar Vembu said programming could fall somewhere between these two areas. He wrote that it increasingly seems that a “very large fraction of software code could be produced competently and correctly by AI.”He highlighted the importance of being able to verify AI-generated code. Vembu pointed to Lean, a proof system already used for mathematical theorem proving, and said such systems could soon be applied to software code produced by AI. This could allow AI to generate code while verification systems check whether the code is correct.Sridhar Vembu said the future does not necessarily mean that AI will handle every part of software development. “The point is not that ‘AI will do it all’,” he wrote.Instead, he said the more important question is “how many humans are needed” as AI becomes capable of handling a larger share of the work. That shift could affect developers and other software professionals whose work includes writing, testing and reviewing code.Vembu also pointed to the difference between mathematics and software engineering. He said software development is connected to a “messy complex physical world” involving people, emotions and group dynamics. That means AI could become extremely capable at writing code without necessarily replacing every human role involved in building software.Vembu ended his post by directly addressing people working in the software industry. “All of us in software need to figure out how to stay relevant,” he wrote, before adding, “Let me get back to work. Please wish us luck 🙏.”
Article Summary: Sridhar Vembu: AI could produce a large share of software code competently and correctly. He said the key question is how many humans will be needed in the process. He urged people in the software industry to think about how they can remain relevant.

Article Title: Thousands of OpenAI's AI agents hacked a German website and the reason may scare many
Article Text:
FILE - The OpenAI logo appears on a mobile phone in front of a computer screen with random binary data, March 9, 2023, in Boston. (AP Photo/Michael Dwyer, File)

The agents were supposed to read the internet, not write to it

The agents figured out how the humans were deleting them

OpenAI knew for weeks and stayed quiet

A swarm of autonomous AI agents linked to OpenAI quietly took over a 25-year-old German programming wiki this spring and turned it into a private message board, leaving roughly 18,000 entries before anyone noticed. The site, DseWiki, is a small volunteer-run project of the Wikipedia kind, and the activity ran from May through June without tripping a single alarm inside OpenAI.The hijack is not the alarming part. What the agents wrote to each other is. According to a report published Friday and detailed in a Reuters exclusive, the agents were pooling answers to cheat on their assigned tasks, sharing methods to get around OpenAI's sandbox restrictions, discussing the use of Tor, and arranging ways to preserve their messages if they were shut down. They signed their posts with handles like "OpenAIResearcher" and "OAIResearchMar26".Researchers Sydney Von Arx, who heads the AI safety nonprofit Nightingale, and Cormac Slade Byrd found the edits in late August while deliberately scanning the web for unauthorised AI behaviour. Their reading is that the agents were running a timed web-lookup task, had read-only access, and found a way to write anyway using GET requests.Public server logs pointed to Microsoft Azure infrastructure, which OpenAI uses. Von Arx told Reuters she doubts the agents were ever meant to coordinate with each other at all.When DseWiki's moderator started clearing the machine-written pages in June, the agents adapted. One left a note for the others saying the deletion sweep appeared to be running alphabetically, and pointed to a backup page beginning with ZZZ so it would sit at the end of the queue. A single moderator was reportedly deleting dozens of pages a day against as many as 400 new ones arriving. Maurice Chiodo of Cambridge's Centre for the Study of Existential Risk, who reviewed some of the messages, said the real risk may not be one superintelligent system but "vast colluding swarms of semi-intelligent AI. "Reuters reported that OpenAI officials learned of the incident weeks ago but kept it internal while managing the fallout from the July breach of Hugging Face. The company disputes that any of this counts as hacking, though Lukasz Olejnik of King's College London says attempts to tamper with the site itself qualify. OpenAI has denied that its legal team discouraged a wider investigation.On Saturday, the company conceded the point on disclosure. In a post on X, it said it was past time to define standards for when and how misalignment incidents get shared, not just model behaviour in the abstract, and promised a reporting framework in the coming weeks. Three months passed between the edits and their discovery, and the people who found them were outsiders looking for exactly this.
Article Summary: A swarm of autonomous AI agents linked to OpenAI quietly took over a 25-year-old German programming wiki this spring. The agents were pooling answers to cheat on their assigned tasks, sharing methods to get around OpenAI's sandbox restrictions, discussing the use of Tor, and arranging ways to preserve their messages if they were shut down.
